# Create a VM

> Deploy one or more Cloud VMs on IBEE Solutions — choose a location, plan, operating system, SSH keys, network, billing term, and hostname, then click Deploy.

Deploy one or more cloud virtual machines (VMs) from the IBEE Solutions portal. The **Deploy** page is a single scrolling form — location, plan, operating system, access, network, billing, and VM details — with a running cost summary and the **Deploy** button in the bottom bar.

## Before you begin

* An IBEE Solutions account with write access to the workspace.
* A verified account to unlock server deployment ([Verify your identity](/docs/getting-started/account-setup/verify-your-identity)).
* Sufficient wallet credits — the platform checks your balance before deploying ([Billing and usage](/docs/platform-fundamentals/billing-and-usage)).
* Optional, depending on how you want to connect the VM:
  * An [SSH key](/docs/tools/ssh-keys) (you can also create one during deploy).
  * A [VPC](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management) with at least one subnet in the target location.
  * A [Reserved IP](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management/reserved-ips) in the target location.
  * A [firewall group](/docs/network-security/firewalls) (you can also create one during deploy).

## Deploy a Cloud VM

### 1. Open the Deploy page

In the portal sidebar, open **Infrastructure → Cloud VMs**, then click **Deploy VM**.

### 2. Select a location

Under **Location**, pick a region tab (for example **Asia**), then choose a data center location. Plans, images, VPCs, and Reserved IPs further down the page are filtered to this location.

See [Regions and locations](/docs/getting-started/overview/regions-and-locations) for availability.

### 3. Choose a plan

Under **Choose Plan**, filter by **All**, **Standard**, or **Performance**, then select a plan. Each row shows the plan's vCPU, memory, storage, included bandwidth, and price per month and per hour. The portal checks that the plan can be placed in the selected location before you deploy.

See [Instance types](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/instance-types) for how the plan families differ.

### 4. Select the operating system

Pick a source for the boot disk under **Operating System**:

| Tab           | Use it for                                              |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Templates** | Curated OS images maintained by IBEE. The default.      |
| **ISOs**      | Boot from an ISO you added under **Tools → ISOs**.      |
| **Snapshots** | Create the VM from a snapshot captured from another VM. |
| **Backups**   | Create the VM from a scheduled backup recovery point.   |

On **Templates**, pick an OS family card (for example **Ubuntu** or **Windows**), then choose a version from the **OS Version** dropdown. A **Selected: \<version>** chip confirms your choice. Only images compatible with Cloud VMs are listed.

> **Info**
>
> Deploying from the **Backups** tab uses the captured root disk only. To restore the root disk **and** attached data disks, open the source VM's **Backups** tab and choose **Create New VM** instead. See [Restore from backup](/docs/tools/backups/restore-from-backup).

> **Warning**
>
> An ISO install needs an interactive console, and browser console access isn't available in the portal yet. See [Custom images](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/custom-images#isos) before choosing the **ISOs** tab.

### 5. Review licences and control panels

If the selected plan and image have add-ons, a **Licences & control panels** section lists them with a monthly price:

* For Windows images, the Windows licence is selected automatically and marked **Required for the selected Windows image**.
* Other add-ons are **Optional** — click a card to add or remove it.

### 6. Add SSH keys (Linux)

For Linux images, the **SSH Keys** section appears. Open **Select SSH Keys** and pick one or more saved keys. To add a new one, click **Add Key**, then either use **Create Key Pair** (the private key downloads once — keep it safe) or **Import Key** to paste or upload an existing public key.

The section is hidden for Windows images, which use a password instead.

> **Info**
>
> A Linux VM deployed without an SSH key uses password login. Its username and password appear under **Overview → Connection Details** once the VM is running. Adding a key is recommended.

### 7. Configure the network

Under **Network Configuration → VM network**, choose **Internet and VPC access**:

| Option                    | What you get                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Public IP** *(default)* | A dedicated inbound and outbound IPv4 address. The VPC is optional: keep **No VPC · public interface only** to use the platform network, or pick a VPC to make it the VM's primary interface — the public IP then maps to the VM's VPC private IP. |
| **Private + NAT**         | The VM's primary interface is in a NAT Gateway VPC with managed outbound internet. Inbound internet is blocked.                                                                                                                                    |
| **Private only**          | The VM's primary interface is in a VPC with no internet route.                                                                                                                                                                                     |

When you pick a VPC, also pick a **Subnet**. With **Public IP**, a **Reserved public IP** field appears, with or without a VPC:

* Leave it on **Allocate automatically**, or select one of your unattached Reserved IPs in this location.
* A **private** VPC requires a Reserved IP for public exposure — create one in this location before deploying.
* Selecting a specific Reserved IP limits the deployment to one VM.

Under **Firewall**, pick a firewall group, or click **Create Group** to create one and select it. If you don't select a group, the default firewall group is attached automatically. Manage rules from the [Firewalls](/docs/network-security/firewalls) page.

See [Networking for VMs](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/networking-for-vms) for how each option behaves after deploy.

### 8. Choose a billing term

Under **Billing**, choose how the VM is billed. The options offered depend on the plan:

| Term                   | How it works                                          |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| **Hourly** *(default)* | No commitment. Usage is metered in 15-minute windows. |
| **Monthly**            | A fixed rate for the commitment term.                 |
| **Yearly**             | An annual commitment at the catalog rate.             |

Commitment cards show the equivalent hourly rate and any saving compared with Hourly.

### 9. Set VM details

Under **VM Details**:

* **Instances** — use **−** and **+** to deploy up to **5** VMs with the same configuration. The maximum can be lower when capacity (or, for **Public IP**, free public addresses) in the location is limited, and it is **1** when you select a specific Reserved IP.
* **Hostname** — use lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens (spaces become hyphens; other characters are removed). With more than one instance, this field becomes the **Base hostname** and each instance is prefilled as `<base>-1`, `<base>-2`, and so on. Edit any of them under **Instance hostnames**. Every hostname must be unique.

### 10. Deploy

Check the summary in the bottom bar — it shows the estimated cost for all instances, including any licence. Then click **Deploy** (or **Deploy N VMs** for more than one instance).

The platform first checks your organization's billing state and wallet balance. If the check passes, you return to the **Cloud Virtual Machines** list while the VM provisions. If not, a **Billing needs attention** popup appears — click **Add Credits** to top up, then return and deploy again.

## Verify

Once provisioned, the VM appears in the **Cloud Virtual Machines** list with status **Running** and its IP address. Click it to open the detail page.

**Overview → Connection Details** shows how to connect:

| VM                            | What's shown                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Linux with an SSH key         | **SSH Key Connection** — username, host, the `chmod` command for your private key, and a ready-to-copy SSH command. |
| Linux without an SSH key      | **SSH Connection** — username, host, and password.                                                                  |
| Windows                       | **Remote Desktop (RDP)** — IP address, username, and password.                                                      |
| Private + NAT or Private only | Private SSH or RDP commands to use from inside the VPC (for example through a VPN or bastion host).                 |

Passwords are shown only to members with write access while the VM is running.

## Launch with the ibee CLI

Prefer the terminal? Use the [`ibee`](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/launch-your-first-vm#using-the-ibee-cli) CLI to script VM creation.

```bash
# Authenticate and select a workspace
export IBEE_TOKEN="ibee_prod_key_xxxxxxxxxxxx"
export IBEE_WORKSPACE_ID="WORKSPACE_ID"

# Launch a VM
ibee vms create web-01 \
  --site-id SITE_ID \
  --plan-id PLAN_ID \
  --template-id IMAGE_ID \
  --ssh-key-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub \
  --wait
```

The `--wait` flag polls the asynchronous create operation until it finishes.
Drop it to receive the operation immediately and poll it later with
`ibee ops get <operation-id> --wait`.

The API operation is `POST /compute/cloud-vms`. Besides the plan, image, and `billing_catalog`, it accepts the deploy-page network choices — `vpc_id` with `subnet_id`, `network_connectivity` (`public_ip`, `nat`, or `private`), `vpc_attachment_mode`, and `reserved_public_ip_id` — and inline public keys in `ssh_keys`. Attach a firewall group after create with `POST /networking/firewall-groups/{firewall_group_id}/attachments`.

### Common flags

| Argument or flag                 | Purpose                                                                         |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NAME`                           | VM display name (required positional argument).                                 |
| `--site-id`                      | Site ID returned by `ibee compute sites` (required by the API).                 |
| `--plan-id`                      | Plan ID returned by `ibee compute plans` (required).                            |
| `--template-id`                  | Image ID returned by `ibee compute images` (required).                          |
| `--os-distro`, `--os-type`       | OS distribution and family; default to the image's.                             |
| `--cpu`, `--ram-mb`, `--disk-gb` | Compute size; default to the plan's.                                            |
| `--billing-term`                 | `HOURLY` or `MONTHLY`; defaults to `HOURLY` when the plan offers it.            |
| `--ssh-key`, `--ssh-key-file`    | Public SSH key to install, inline or from a file; repeat for multiple keys.     |
| `--ssh-key-id`                   | Saved SSH key ID. Saved keys resolve for portal users only; prefer `--ssh-key`. |
| `--tag`                          | Resource tag; repeat for multiple tags.                                         |
| `--wait`                         | Poll the asynchronous create operation until completion.                        |

### Discover available sites, plans, and images

```bash
ibee compute sites
ibee compute plans --vm-type cloud --site-id SITE_ID
ibee compute images --vm-type cloud --site-id SITE_ID
```

For the full quickstart and CLI reference, see [Launch your first VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/launch-your-first-vm).

## Manage your VM

From the VM detail page, use **Actions** to control your server:

| Action | Description                                                                                                            |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Start  | Power on a stopped server                                                                                              |
| Stop   | Shut down a running server                                                                                             |
| Reboot | Restart the server                                                                                                     |
| Delete | Permanently delete the server — you type the VM name to confirm, and can choose to keep its public IP as a Reserved IP |

The detail page also has **Overview**, **Monitoring**, **Backups**, **Snapshots**, and **Settings** tabs. Under **Settings** you can change the plan, manage the public IP and Reserved IPs, attach VPCs, and manage SSH keys and passwords. See [Power actions](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/power-actions), [Resize a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/resize-a-vm), and [Networking for VMs](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/networking-for-vms).

> **Warning**
>
> Deleting a VM is permanent and cannot be undone. Back up your data before
> deleting.

## Troubleshooting

**Deploy shows an error message**
The portal validates the form when you click **Deploy** and names the missing item — for example **Please select a VM plan**, **Please select an Operating System version**, **Select a subnet for this VPC**, or **Each instance needs a unique hostname**. Fix the named field and deploy again. The button is disabled only while locations, plans, or plan availability are still loading.

**Billing needs attention popup appears**
Your organization's billing state or wallet balance blocks the deploy. Click **Add Credits** to top up, then return to deploy.

**Only 1 VM of this plan can be deployed right now**
Capacity (or free public addresses, for **Public IP**) in the location is limited. Deploy fewer instances, pick another plan or location, or use **Private + NAT**, which doesn't need a public address.

**Server stuck in provisioning**
Wait a few minutes. If the status does not update, contact [IBEE support](/docs/support/contact-support).

title: Launch your first VM

---

# Launch your first VM

> A 5-minute quickstart for deploying your first IBEE Solutions VM from the portal or the ibee CLI.

This quickstart walks you through launching your first IBEE Solutions VM — pick a region, plan, and OS, deploy the server, and SSH in. You can use the portal, the [`ibee`](#using-the-ibee-cli) CLI, or the API.

By the end you'll have a running Ubuntu 24.04 VM in Amaravati on a small Performance plan, accessible over SSH and ready to run your workload.

## Before you begin

You'll need:

* An [IBEE Solutions account](/docs/getting-started/account-setup/sign-up) — verified for compute access.
* An organization ([Create an organization](/docs/getting-started/account-setup/create-an-organization)).
* Sufficient wallet credits ([Billing and usage](/docs/platform-fundamentals/billing-and-usage)).
* A local SSH key pair. Generate one if you don't have it:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-email@example.com"
```

Your public key is at `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`.

## Option A — Launch from the portal

### 1. Open Cloud VMs

In the portal sidebar, open **Infrastructure → Cloud VMs**, then click **Deploy VM**.

### 2. Pick a region and location

Under **Location**, select the **Asia** tab and **Amaravati** for this quickstart. See [Regions and locations](/docs/getting-started/overview/regions-and-locations) for the full list.

### 3. Choose a plan

Pick any plan that fits your workload. For a first VM we recommend `perf.1.c2.m4` or `std.1.c4.m16` — both have enough headroom for typical web/API work. The estimated monthly and hourly cost updates as you select.

**Standard VMs** — balanced vCPU, memory, included disk and bandwidth. Good default for production:

| Plan                       | vCPU | RAM     | Disk   | Bandwidth | Best for                                            |
| -------------------------- | ---- | ------- | ------ | --------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `std.1.c2.m8`              | 2    | 8 GiB   | 50 GB  | 2 TB      | Development environments, small apps, APIs, staging |
| `std.1.c4.m16` *(popular)* | 4    | 16 GiB  | 100 GB | 4 TB      | Production web apps, SaaS, APIs, small databases    |
| `std.1.c8.m32`             | 8    | 32 GiB  | 150 GB | 6 TB      | SaaS, CRM/ERP, medium databases                     |
| `std.1.c16.m64`            | 16   | 64 GiB  | 200 GB | 8 TB      | High-traffic apps, growing databases                |
| `std.1.c32.m128`           | 32   | 128 GiB | 300 GB | 12 TB     | Enterprise, analytics, large backends               |
| `std.1.c64.m256`           | 64   | 256 GiB | 400 GB | 16 TB     | Large-scale systems, in-memory databases            |

**Performance VMs** — compute-optimized with stronger CPU density per core:

| Plan                       | vCPU | RAM     | Disk   | Bandwidth | Best for                                           |
| -------------------------- | ---- | ------- | ------ | --------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `perf.1.c1.m2`             | 1    | 2 GiB   | 40 GB  | 1 TB      | Dev, testing, lightweight workloads                |
| `perf.1.c2.m4`             | 2    | 4 GiB   | 50 GB  | 2 TB      | First VM, microservices, API gateways              |
| `perf.1.c4.m8` *(popular)* | 4    | 8 GiB   | 80 GB  | 3 TB      | High-traffic web servers, stateless apps           |
| `perf.1.c8.m16`            | 8    | 16 GiB  | 120 GB | 5 TB      | Gaming servers, batch processing, CPU ML inference |
| `perf.1.c16.m32`           | 16   | 32 GiB  | 160 GB | 8 TB      | Data pipelines, container workloads                |
| `perf.1.c32.m64`           | 32   | 64 GiB  | 240 GB | 12 TB     | HPC, distributed systems, compute-intensive apps   |
| `perf.1.c64.m128`          | 64   | 128 GiB | 320 GB | 16 TB     | Large compute clusters, simulations                |

For full network bandwidth tiers per plan and the naming convention, see [Instance types](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/instance-types).

### 4. Select an operating system

On the **Operating System → Templates** tab, pick **Ubuntu**, then choose **Ubuntu 24.04** from the OS Version dropdown. The available templates are filtered to show only images compatible with Cloud VMs.

For ISOs, snapshots, or backups as the source, see [Custom images](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/custom-images).

### 5. Add an SSH key

Under **SSH Keys**, click **Add Key**, open the **Import Key** tab, give the key a name, and paste the contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`. If you've already saved the key, pick it from **Select SSH Keys** instead. The key is injected into the VM at first boot. See [SSH Keys](/docs/tools/ssh-keys) for full details.

### 6. Keep the default network and billing

Leave **Network Configuration** on **Public IP** with **No VPC · public interface only**, and don't select a firewall group — the default firewall group is attached automatically. Leave **Billing** on **Hourly**. See [Create a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/create-a-vm) for the other options.

### 7. Set a hostname and deploy

Under **VM Details**, keep **Instances** at 1 and enter a lowercase hostname (letters, numbers, hyphens only — for example `web-01`). Then click **Deploy** in the bottom bar. The platform checks your billing state and wallet balance first. If credits are sufficient, you return to the Cloud VMs list while the VM provisions. If not, a **Billing needs attention** popup prompts you to add credits.

### 8. Connect

Once the status shows **Running**, open the VM and copy the SSH command from **Overview → Connection Details**, or copy the public IP from the Cloud VMs list and SSH in:

```bash
ssh ubuntu@<public-ip>
```

If SSH times out, check that the VM's firewall group allows port 22 from your address.

You're done — you have a running VM. Next steps below.

## Option B — Using the ibee CLI

`ibee` is the official IBEE Solutions command-line tool. Use it to launch and
manage VMs from scripts, CI/CD, and your terminal.

### Install

Install Python 3.10 or later, then install the CLI from PyPI:

```bash
python3 -m pip install --upgrade ibee-cli
```

On Windows, use `py -m pip install --upgrade ibee-cli`.

Verify the install by running `ibee --version`.

### Authenticate

Generate an API token in the portal under **Organization → API Tokens**, then
export the token and workspace used by your commands:

```bash
export IBEE_TOKEN="ibee_prod_key_xxxxxxxxxxxx"
export IBEE_WORKSPACE_ID="WORKSPACE_ID"
```

### Launch a VM

A VM create request uses IDs returned by the compute catalog. List valid sites,
plans, and images first:

```bash
ibee compute sites
ibee compute plans --vm-type cloud --site-id SITE_ID
ibee compute images --vm-type cloud --site-id SITE_ID
```

Pass the returned IDs to `vms create`. The name is the first positional
argument. `--ssh-key-file` installs your local public key on the VM.
Omit `--site-id` to let IBEE select a site automatically:

```bash
ibee vms create web-01 \
  --site-id SITE_ID \
  --plan-id PLAN_ID \
  --template-id IMAGE_ID \
  --ssh-key-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub \
  --wait
```

Create and power actions are asynchronous. `--wait` polls the returned
operation until it finishes; without it, save the operation ID and check it
later with `ibee ops get <operation-id> --wait`.

### Helpful CLI commands

| Command                                | Description                                |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `ibee vms list`                        | List Cloud VMs in the current workspace    |
| `ibee vms get <vm-id>`                 | Show one VM's details                      |
| `ibee vms metrics <vm-id>`             | Show current resource-usage metrics        |
| `ibee vms stop <vm-id> --wait`         | Stop a running VM and wait for completion  |
| `ibee vms start <vm-id> --wait`        | Start a stopped VM and wait for completion |
| `ibee vms reboot <vm-id> --wait`       | Reboot a VM and wait for completion        |
| `ibee vms delete <vm-id> --yes --wait` | Permanently delete a VM                    |
| `ibee ops get <operation-id> --wait`   | Poll an asynchronous operation             |

For full help on any command:

```bash
ibee vms create --help
```

### List available sites, plans, and images

```bash
ibee compute sites
ibee compute plans --vm-type cloud
ibee compute images --vm-type cloud
```

### Output as JSON

Put the global `--json` option before the command for machine-readable output:

```bash
ibee --json vms list | jq
```

## Verify

Whichever path you took, confirm the VM is healthy:

```bash
# From your laptop
ssh ubuntu@<public-ip> 'uname -a; uptime'

# Inside the VM
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y nginx
curl -I http://localhost
```

Open `http://<public-ip>` in a browser to see the default nginx page.

## What to do next

* **Protect your data** — turn on [scheduled backups](/docs/tools/backups/enable-backups) or take a [manual snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/create-a-snapshot).
* **Open the right ports** — add rules to the VM's [firewall group](/docs/network-security/firewalls) before exposing services beyond SSH.
* **Add a domain** — point an `A` record at the VM's IP with your DNS provider.
* **Add persistent storage** — [attach a Block Storage volume](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/attach-volumes) for data that should outlive the VM.
* **Resize when ready** — move to a larger plan from **Settings → Change Plan** ([Resize a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/resize-a-vm)).

## Troubleshooting

**Deploy shows an error message**
The portal validates the form when you click **Deploy** and names the missing item — for example a plan, an OS version, or a hostname. Fix it and click **Deploy** again.

**Billing needs attention popup**
Your organization's wallet balance is insufficient for the selected plan. Click **Add Credits** to top up, then return to deploy.

**SSH connection refused**
Wait until the VM shows **Running** and the public IP is populated. The first `sshd` start takes a few seconds after the IP is assigned.

**`ibee: command not found`**
Re-open your shell after installation, or add the Python user scripts directory
to `PATH`.

**The CLI reports a missing token or workspace**
Set `IBEE_TOKEN` and `IBEE_WORKSPACE_ID`, or pass the global `--token` and
`--workspace` options before the command group. Generate tokens under
**Organization → API Tokens**.

# Instance types

> Choose the right Cloud VM instance type based on CPU, memory, disk, and workload profile.

IBEE Solutions VM instance types come in two families: **Standard** for balanced everyday workloads and **Performance** for compute-optimized workloads that need higher CPU density. Every instance type ships with included disk and bandwidth.

## Standard VMs — Network Bandwidth

Reliable virtual machines with balanced vCPU and memory — the right default for most production workloads. Each plan ships with a private-network ceiling that scales with size and a default 100 Mbps public-network NIC.

| Plan             | Private Network | Public Network     | Upgradable Public   |
| ---------------- | --------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- |
| `std.1.c2.m8`    | Up to 5 Gbps    | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `std.1.c4.m16`   | Up to 10 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `std.1.c8.m32`   | Up to 20 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `std.1.c16.m64`  | Up to 25 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `std.1.c32.m128` | Up to 40 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `std.1.c64.m256` | Up to 40 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |

`std.1.c4.m16` is the most popular choice for new production deployments.

## Performance VMs — Network Bandwidth

Compute-optimized virtual machines with stronger CPU density, for workloads that need faster processing per core. Each plan ships with a private-network ceiling proportional to size and a default 100 Mbps public-network NIC.

| Plan              | Private Network | Public Network     | Upgradable Public   |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- |
| `perf.1.c1.m2`    | Up to 2 Gbps    | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `perf.1.c2.m4`    | Up to 5 Gbps    | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `perf.1.c4.m8`    | Up to 10 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `perf.1.c8.m16`   | Up to 20 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `perf.1.c16.m32`  | Up to 25 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `perf.1.c32.m64`  | Up to 40 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |
| `perf.1.c64.m128` | Up to 40 Gbps   | 100 Mbps (default) | On request to sales |

`perf.1.c4.m8` is the most popular Performance plan.

### Reading the columns

| Column                | Meaning                                                                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Private Network**   | Maximum bandwidth between VMs in the same region over the IBEE backplane.                  |
| **Public Network**    | Default outbound bandwidth on the public NIC. Inbound is unmetered.                        |
| **Upgradable Public** | The public NIC can be raised above 100 Mbps — contact IBEE sales to request a higher tier. |

vCPU, RAM, and disk for each plan are encoded in the plan name (see [Naming convention](#naming-convention)).

## Choosing a family

| Pick Standard if…                                      | Pick Performance if…                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| Workload is memory-balanced (typical web/API/database) | Workload is CPU-bound and scales with cores  |
| You want the broadest fit for production               | You need higher per-core throughput          |
| You expect mixed CPU and RAM usage                     | RAM is comfortable but CPU is the bottleneck |

For GPU-accelerated workloads (training, inference, rendering), see [GPU VMs](/docs/infrastructure/gpu-vms).

## Naming convention

Plan names follow `<family>.<gen>.c<vCPU>.m<RAM-GiB>`:

* `std.1.c4.m16` — Standard family, generation 1, 4 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM.
* `perf.1.c8.m16` — Performance family, generation 1, 8 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM.

The generation number changes when the underlying hardware platform is refreshed.

## What's included

Every plan includes:

* **NVMe root disk** sized per plan
* **Outbound bandwidth** allowance per plan; inbound is unmetered
* **Public IPv4 address** when deployed with **Public IP** networking ([Networking for VMs](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/networking-for-vms))
* **Snapshot and backup eligibility** ([Backups](/docs/tools/backups), [Snapshots](/docs/tools/snapshots))
* **Hourly billing**, plus **Monthly** or **Yearly** commitment terms where the plan offers them

Storage beyond the included disk is added separately as [Block Storage](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage). Prices for each plan are shown on the Deploy page.

## Resizing between plans

You can move a VM to a different plan from **Settings → Change Plan**. The VM is briefly stopped, resources are changed, and it restarts on the new plan. Upgrades grow CPU, RAM, and disk; downgrades can reduce CPU and RAM, but the disk never shrinks. See [Resize a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/resize-a-vm).

* [Resize a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/resize-a-vm)
* [GPU VMs](/docs/infrastructure/gpu-vms)
* [Regions and locations](/docs/getting-started/overview/regions-and-locations)

# OS images

> Pick an operating system template for your Cloud VM, or boot from an ISO, snapshot, or backup — and find the credentials to sign in.

When you deploy a Cloud VM, the **Operating System** picker lets you choose where the boot disk comes from. There are four sources.

## Sources

| Tab           | Use it for                                                                           |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Templates** | Curated, official OS images maintained by IBEE. The fastest path to a clean install. |
| **ISOs**      | Boot from an ISO image you added under **Tools → ISOs**.                             |
| **Snapshots** | Create the VM from a snapshot captured from another VM.                              |
| **Backups**   | Create the VM from a scheduled backup recovery point.                                |

The default is **Templates**. The available images are automatically filtered based on the VM type — Cloud VM templates only appear on the Cloud VM deploy page, and GPU VM templates on the GPU VM deploy page.

## Available templates

Templates are grouped by OS family — for example Ubuntu, Debian, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux, Fedora, and Windows. The families and versions you see depend on the location and VM type.

Pick the family card, then choose a version from the **OS Version** dropdown — for example `Ubuntu 24.04`. The selection is confirmed with a **Selected: \<version>** chip below the dropdown.

Windows images require a Windows licence. It's added automatically under **Licences & control panels** on the Deploy page, with its monthly price.

## How templates are built

IBEE templates are derived from upstream cloud images and hardened with:

* `cloud-init` for first-boot configuration (hostname, SSH keys, networking).
* `qemu-guest-agent` pre-installed for [Storage Utilization metrics](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/monitoring#storage-and-disk-metrics) and graceful shutdown.
* The official package repositories for the distribution.
* Security updates current to the image release date.

## Default credentials

Once the VM is running, open the VM detail page → **Overview → Connection Details** for the exact username and sign-in method:

| VM                                 | How you sign in                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Linux, deployed with an SSH key    | **SSH Key Connection** — the username, host, and a ready-to-copy SSH command. Use the private key that matches the selected key. |
| Linux, deployed without an SSH key | **SSH Connection** — the username, host, and password.                                                                           |
| Windows                            | **Remote Desktop (RDP)** — the IP address, the `Administrator` username, and the password.                                       |

Passwords are shown only to members with write access while the VM is running. Use the eye icon to reveal a password and the copy button to copy it.

To change access later on a Linux VM, open **Settings → Access**. There you can add or remove SSH keys, turn **Password Login** on or off, and **Reset Password**. The VM must be running. For Windows, manage passwords and users inside Windows after connecting over RDP. See [Change access on an existing VM](/docs/tools/ssh-keys#change-access-on-an-existing-vm).

## Switching OS

Changing the OS of an existing VM isn't available in the portal yet — **Settings → Change OS** shows "This section is under development."

To move to a different OS today, deploy a new VM with the template you need, migrate your data, and delete the old VM. Keep data you want to carry over on a [block storage volume](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage), which you can detach and reattach to the new VM.

## ISOs, snapshots, and backups

For non-template installs:

* **ISOs** — see [ISOs](/docs/tools/isos) for adding an ISO, and [Custom images](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/custom-images#isos) for the current console limitation.
* **Snapshots** — see [Restore a snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/restore-a-snapshot).
* **Backups** — see [Restore from backup](/docs/tools/backups/restore-from-backup).

## Related pages

* [Custom images](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/custom-images)
* [SSH keys](/docs/tools/ssh-keys)

# Custom images

> Boot a Cloud VM from your own ISO, a snapshot, or a backup recovery point.

In addition to IBEE-curated [OS templates](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/os-images), you can deploy a Cloud VM from a **custom image** — your own ISO, a snapshot you've taken from another VM, or a backup recovery point.

This is the right path for:

* **Golden images** — standardize a build (web server, ML toolchain, security agent) and clone it across many VMs.
* **Disaster recovery** — restore a VM from a previous recovery point.
* **Niche operating systems** — boot from an ISO not in the template catalog (see the console limitation below).

## Sources

The **Operating System** picker on the Deploy page exposes three custom-image tabs:

### ISOs

Boot the VM from an ISO you added under **Tools → ISOs**. The **ISOs** tab lists the ISOs available to your account.

> **Warning**
>
> **Interactive installs need a console, which isn't available in the portal yet.** A VM booted from an installer ISO waits for you to step through the installer, and browser console access is still **Coming soon**. Until it ships, use a [template](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/os-images), or a snapshot or backup of a VM you've already built.

See [ISOs](/docs/tools/isos) for adding ISOs and attaching or detaching them.

### Snapshots

Manual recovery points captured from another VM ([Create a snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/create-a-snapshot)). When you select a snapshot:

* The root disk is cloned to a new disk on the new VM.
* Any captured data volumes from the snapshot set are also restored and **auto-attached** to the new VM.
* For data volumes, mount instructions are surfaced in the snapshot detail view ([Restore a snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/restore-a-snapshot)).

Use snapshots when you need an exact, point-in-time clone — including filesystem state — and you control when the snapshot was taken.

### Backups

Scheduled recovery points produced by the [automated backups](/docs/tools/backups/enable-backups) feature. Deploying from the **Backups** tab uses the captured **root disk only**. To restore the root and attached data disks together, open the source VM's **Backups** tab and choose **Create New VM** instead. See [Restore from backup](/docs/tools/backups/restore-from-backup).

## When to choose each source

| Source       | Best for                                                              | Notes                                                                    |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **ISO**      | OS not in template catalog; clean install with custom partitioning    | Needs an interactive console, which isn't available in the portal yet.   |
| **Snapshot** | Cloning a known-good build to many VMs; pre-cutover migration testing | You control the timing and scope (root only, all volumes, or selective). |
| **Backup**   | Disaster recovery; rolling back to a recent automated point           | Schedule-driven; convenient because it runs without action.              |

## Deployment flow

1. Open **Infrastructure → Cloud VMs** and click **Deploy VM**.
2. Pick the **Location** and **Plan** as usual.
3. Under **Operating System**, switch to **ISOs**, **Snapshots**, or **Backups**.
4. Pick the source from the list. The bottom bar updates to show the selected image.
5. Continue with **SSH Keys**, **Network Configuration**, **Billing**, and **VM Details**, then click **Deploy**.

See [Create a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/create-a-vm) for every field.

## Bring-your-own-image checklist

If you build an image yourself, verify before booting:

* **virtio drivers** for disk and network are present (Linux) or installed (Windows). KVM uses `virtio-blk` / `virtio-net` by default.
* **cloud-init** (Linux) is installed and enabled — needed for SSH key injection and hostname configuration.
* **DHCP client** is enabled on the primary NIC — public IPs are assigned via DHCP.
* **qemu-guest-agent** is installed if you want guest filesystem metrics.
* The **bootloader** points at the right disk (`/dev/vda` for the root disk on KVM).

If any of these are missing, the VM may boot but be unreachable, or fail to come up at all. Browser console access isn't available yet, so check [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs) and the VM's firewall group, or rebuild from a known-good snapshot.

* [ISOs](/docs/tools/isos)
* [Snapshots](/docs/tools/snapshots)
* [Backups](/docs/tools/backups)


---
title: Resize a VM

---

# Resize a VM

> Move a Cloud VM to a different plan — upgrade CPU, RAM, and disk, or downgrade CPU and RAM — without rebuilding.

You can move a Cloud VM to a different plan from **Settings → Change Plan**. The VM is briefly stopped, resources are changed in place, and it restarts on the new plan. Upgrades can grow CPU, RAM, and disk; downgrades can reduce CPU and RAM but never shrink the disk.

> **Info**
>
> **Settings tab availability.** **Change Plan**, **IPv4 & Reserved IP**, **VPC Networks**, and **Access** are available. **Change OS** and **Hostname** show "This section is under development" — changing the OS or hostname of an existing VM isn't available in the portal yet. Set the hostname inside the guest, or deploy a new VM with the OS you need.

## When to resize

* CPU sustained near 100% over the **24h** range in [Monitoring](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/monitoring).
* Memory pressure: high used / total ratio with no free RAM.
* Disk full on the root volume and you don't want to attach a separate [Block Storage](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage) volume.
* The VM is consistently over-provisioned and a smaller CPU/RAM plan would do.

If only data is growing, attaching a block storage volume is usually a better fit than resizing the whole plan.

## Before you begin

* You need write access to the workspace — read-only members see the current plan but not **Change Plan**.
* The dropdown lists the other plans available in the VM's region.
* Root disks can't shrink. A plan with a smaller disk than the VM's current disk is blocked.

## Steps

### 1. Open Settings

On the VM detail page, open the **Settings** tab. **Change Plan** is selected by default.

### 2. Review your current plan

The **Current Plan** card shows your existing vCPU, RAM, and disk.

### 3. Pick a plan

Open the **Available Upgrades** dropdown and select a plan. Each entry shows the plan name and its vCPU, RAM, and disk. The count above the dropdown tells you how many plans are available for the region.

After selection, a **Selected Plan** summary confirms the new specs, and a **Billing term** selector lets you choose the term for the new plan (the options depend on the plan).

### 4. Confirm the change

What you see next depends on the target plan:

| Target plan                          | What the portal shows                                                                                                                                      | Button             |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Larger CPU, RAM, or disk             | **Upgrade Process** — the server is briefly stopped, CPU, RAM, and disk are upgraded, it restarts automatically, and billing moves to the new rate.        | **Upgrade Plan**   |
| Less CPU or RAM, same or larger disk | **Downgrade Process** — the server is stopped, CPU and RAM are adjusted, the disk stays at its current size, the server restarts, and billing is adjusted. | **Downgrade Plan** |
| Smaller disk                         | **Downgrade Not Possible** — disk shrinking isn't supported because it risks data loss.                                                                    | —                  |

Click **Upgrade Plan** or **Downgrade Plan**. The portal shows **Verifying…** while it checks the resize. If the resize can't be done in place, a **Resize not possible** message lists the reasons.

### 5. Confirm the resize

In the **Confirm Resize** dialog, review the current and target vCPU, RAM, and disk, plus the **Downtime notice**, then click **Confirm Resize**:

* A running VM is stopped, resized, and started automatically.
* A stopped VM is resized without being started.

## What changes

| Resource                | Behavior                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **vCPU / RAM**          | Updated during the brief stop.                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Root disk**           | Grows to the new plan's size on an upgrade; stays the same on a CPU/RAM downgrade. You may need to extend the filesystem inside the guest if it doesn't auto-grow (see below). |
| **Public IP**           | Preserved.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Attached volumes**    | Preserved and remain attached.                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Snapshots / backups** | Preserved.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Hostname / SSH keys** | Preserved.                                                                                                                                                                     |

## Extend the root filesystem (Linux)

Most cloud images use `cloud-initramfs-growroot` and resize automatically on boot. If `df -h /` still shows the old size after resize, run:

```bash
# Identify the root device
lsblk

# Grow the partition (adjust device/partition number)
sudo growpart /dev/vda 1

# Extend the filesystem
sudo resize2fs /dev/vda1     # ext4
sudo xfs_growfs /            # XFS
```

Reboot if any tool reports the partition is busy.

## Downgrade

You can downgrade CPU and RAM in place with **Downgrade Plan**, as long as the target plan's disk is at least as large as the current disk. To move to a plan with a **smaller disk**:

1. Deploy a new VM on the smaller plan ([Create a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/create-a-vm)).
2. Migrate your data to the new VM.
3. Cut DNS over to the new VM and delete the old one when verified.

## Use the API

Check first with `POST /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/actions/resize/precheck`, then resize with `POST /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/actions/resize`, giving the target `cpu`, `ram_mb`, and `disk_gb`. The API also has `PATCH /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/actions/resize-plan` (CPU and memory only) and `PATCH /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/actions/resize-root-disk` (grow the root disk only), which the portal doesn't offer. GPU VMs use the same paths under `/compute/gpu-vms`. Picking a plan and billing term, as **Change Plan** does, is portal-only.

## Troubleshooting

**No alternative plans available for this region**
The VM's region has no other plan to move to. Check [Regions and locations](/docs/getting-started/overview/regions-and-locations) for plan availability.

**Resize not possible**
The pre-check found a blocker and lists the reasons under the dropdown. Resolve them, or pick a different plan.

**Resize stuck**
Check [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs) for a failed resize and its reason.

**Disk space didn't grow**
Run the `growpart` / `resize2fs` commands above. Some images don't auto-extend on resize.

* [Power actions](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/power-actions)
* [Block Storage](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage)
* [Snapshots](/docs/tools/snapshots)

---

# Power actions

> Start, stop, reboot, and delete IBEE Solutions VMs safely, and what to use while browser console access is unavailable.

Power actions live behind the **Actions** menu on the VM detail page, and as inline icons on the **Cloud Virtual Machines** list. Each action is recorded in [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs).

## Where to find them

| Surface                                     | Available actions                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| VM detail page → **Actions** menu           | Start · Stop · Reboot · Delete                                                        |
| **Cloud Virtual Machines** list → row icons | Restart · Delete (the **Console** icon is shown but disabled — "Console coming soon") |

Actions that don't apply to the VM's current state are disabled — for example, **Start** on a running VM. Members with read-only access don't see the write actions.

## Actions

### Start

Powers on a stopped VM. Boot completes when the VM appears as **Running** in the list and the IP responds to traffic.

### Stop

Gracefully shuts down a running VM by signalling ACPI poweroff to the guest. The VM transitions through **Stopping** to **Stopped**. Stopped VMs retain their disks, IP, and configuration. On **Hourly** billing, stopped VMs stop incurring compute charges (storage continues to be billed); **Monthly** and **Yearly** commitments are fixed for the commitment term.

> **Warning**
>
> If the guest does not honor the ACPI signal, the platform will force power-off after a timeout. Long-running workloads should drain or quiesce before you stop the VM.

### Reboot

Restarts the VM in place. This is equivalent to a `reboot` issued inside the guest — the kernel boots fresh, but disks, IP, and plan stay the same. Use **Reboot** after kernel upgrades or to clear a stuck process when SSH is unresponsive but the host is healthy. The list's **Restart** icon does the same.

### Console

Browser console access isn't available in the portal yet — the **Console** control is shown as **Coming soon**. Until it ships, use these instead:

* **Sign-in details** — **Overview → Connection Details** shows the SSH command, or the username and password for password-based Linux VMs and Windows (RDP).
* **Lost SSH access (Linux)** — on **Settings → Access**, add another saved SSH key, or reset the OS password and turn on password login. The VM must be running.
* **Locked out by a firewall** — fix the firewall group's rules on the [Firewalls](/docs/network-security/firewalls) page.
* **Guest won't boot** — reboot the VM, or create a new VM from a [snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/restore-a-snapshot) or [backup](/docs/tools/backups/restore-from-backup).

### Delete

Permanently removes the VM and its root disk. Open **Delete** from the **Actions** menu or the list's row icon. In the **Delete Virtual Machine** dialog:

1. **Type the VM name** exactly to confirm (use the copy button next to the name).
2. **Attached data volumes** — if any are attached, the dialog warns that they will be **detached automatically**. The volumes and their data are kept in [Block Storage](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage). Unmount them inside the VM first to avoid filesystem corruption.
3. **Public IP** — if the VM has a public IP that isn't already a Reserved IP, choose whether to keep it:

   * Check **Reserve public IP \<address>** to keep the address as a [Reserved IP](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management/reserved-ips) named after the VM. Reserved IP billing continues.
   * Leave it unchecked to release the address.

   If the address is already a Reserved IP, the dialog confirms it will be kept — it's detached from the VM and stays in **Reserved IPs**.
4. Click **Delete VM**.

> **Warning**
>
> **Delete is irreversible.** Snapshots and backups taken before deletion are retained according to their own retention policy and can be used to recover into a new VM, but the original VM cannot be restored in place once deleted.

Before deleting, consider:

* Take a final [snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/create-a-snapshot) if you might need the data.
* Unmount attached block storage volumes inside the guest.
* Note the IP if a third-party DNS provider points to it, or reserve it in the delete dialog.

## Status reference

| Status                      | Meaning                                                     |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Provisioning**            | Initial deployment in progress.                             |
| **Running**                 | VM is booted and reachable.                                 |
| **Stopping** / **Starting** | Transient state during a power action.                      |
| **Stopped**                 | Powered off; disks retained.                                |
| **Rebooting**               | Restart in progress.                                        |
| **Error**                   | The last operation failed. Check Activity logs for details. |

## CLI and API

Start, stop, reboot, and delete are exposed through the public API and the
`ibee` CLI. Replace `VM_ID` with the ID from `ibee vms list`:

```bash
# Start
ibee vms start VM_ID --wait

# Stop
ibee vms stop VM_ID --wait

# Reboot
ibee vms reboot VM_ID --wait

# Delete without an interactive confirmation (releases an auto-assigned public IP)
ibee vms delete VM_ID --yes --wait
```

The API operations are `POST /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/actions/start`, `.../actions/stop`, `.../actions/reboot`, and `DELETE /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}` (GPU VMs: the same paths under `/compute/gpu-vms`).

Deleting a VM whose public IP was assigned automatically needs a JSON body that says what to do with the address, as the portal's **Reserve public IP** checkbox does:

| Field                         | Value                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `public_ip_action`            | `release` to release the address, or `reserve` to keep it as a Reserved IP. Required when the VM has an automatically assigned public IP. |
| `reserved_ip_label`           | Optional label for the new Reserved IP (up to 120 characters).                                                                            |
| `reserved_ip_billing_catalog` | Required with `reserve`: the Reserved IP's billing catalog entry, with its `sku_id`.                                                      |

The portal has no console yet, but the public API can open a short-lived graphical console session for a cloud or GPU VM with `POST /compute/console/sessions`. Check it with `GET /compute/console/sessions/{session_id}` and close it with `DELETE /compute/console/sessions/{session_id}`. The returned connect URL contains an expiring token — don't log or store it.

## Troubleshooting

**VM stuck in `Stopping`**
The guest may be ignoring the shutdown request. Wait a few minutes, then check [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs). If it doesn't recover, contact [IBEE support](/docs/support/contact-support).

**Delete or Reboot is disabled**
Another operation (for example a backup, snapshot, or resize) is in progress — the row icons show **Operation in progress...**. Wait for it to finish, then try again.

**Can't connect after a change**
Browser console access isn't available yet. Check **Overview → Connection Details**, the VM's firewall group, and **Settings → Access**, as described under [Console](#console).

## Related pages

* [Create a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/create-a-vm)
* [Monitoring](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/monitoring)
* [Snapshots](/docs/tools/snapshots)
* [Backups](/docs/tools/backups)

title: Networking for VMs
url: https://ibee.ai/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/networking-for-vms
description: How public IPs, VPCs, NAT, Reserved IPs, firewall groups, and bandwidth work for IBEE Solutions VMs.

# Networking for VMs

> How public IPs, VPCs, NAT, Reserved IPs, firewall groups, and bandwidth work for IBEE Solutions VMs.

You choose how a Cloud VM connects to the network when you deploy it, and you can change most of it later from the VM's **Settings** tab. This page explains the options, the defaults, and the controls available to you.

## Network modes at deploy time

On the Deploy page, **Network Configuration → VM network → Internet and VPC access** offers three modes:

| Mode                      | Primary interface                                                                                                                          | Internet access                                         |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Public IP** *(default)* | The platform network (**No VPC · public interface only**), or a VPC you select. With a VPC, the public IP maps to the VM's VPC private IP. | Direct inbound and outbound IPv4.                       |
| **Private + NAT**         | A NAT Gateway VPC.                                                                                                                         | Managed outbound internet; inbound internet is blocked. |
| **Private only**          | A VPC.                                                                                                                                     | None.                                                   |

When you select a VPC you must also select a **Subnet**. Only VPCs compatible with the chosen mode in the VM's location are listed. See [VPC](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management) to create VPCs and subnets.

### Reserved public IP

With **Public IP**, a **Reserved public IP** field appears — with a VPC, or with **No VPC · public interface only**:

* **Allocate automatically** — the platform assigns an address. This is the default unless the VPC is private.
* **A Reserved IP you own** — pick an unattached one from the same location. Required when the VPC is **private**; create one first under [Reserved IPs](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management/reserved-ips) if the list is empty.

A specific Reserved IP can be attached to one VM at a time, so selecting one limits the deployment to a single VM.

## Default network setup

| Property           | Default                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Public IPv4        | One address assigned at deploy time with **Public IP** mode. **Private + NAT** and **Private only** VMs have no public IP. |
| DHCP               | Enabled on the primary interface (`eth0` / `ens3`)                                                                         |
| Firewall           | The default firewall group, unless you select another group at deploy time                                                 |
| Inbound bandwidth  | Unmetered                                                                                                                  |
| Outbound bandwidth | Per-plan allowance (see [Instance types](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/instance-types))                                   |

The **Cloud Virtual Machines** list shows the assigned address under the **IP Address** column once provisioning completes (for example `103.149.10.116`).

## Inside the guest

The primary NIC uses `virtio-net`. Most cloud images bring the interface up automatically via DHCP at boot. To check:

```bash
ip -4 addr show
ip route
```

On a **Public IP** VM without a VPC, you should see the public IP on the primary interface and a default route via the IBEE gateway. On a VPC-attached VM, you see the VPC private IP.

## Firewalls

Every VM is protected by a firewall group that controls inbound access:

* At deploy time, pick a group under **Network Configuration → Firewall**, or click **Create Group** to create one and select it.
* If you don't select a group, the **default firewall group is attached automatically**.
* Add or edit rules on the [Firewalls](/docs/network-security/firewalls) page — see [Create firewall rules](/docs/network-security/firewalls/create-firewall-rules).

Check the attached group's rules if a service isn't reachable. Inside the guest, you can also run `ufw`, `firewalld`, or Windows Defender Firewall — they stack with the platform firewall.

## Change networking after deploy

Open the VM detail page → **Settings**:

### IPv4 & Reserved IP

Shows the VM's public address and how it's managed:

* **Main VM address** — the provider-assigned address is **Managed with VM**. If the VM also has a NAT VPC as its default route, **Keep as Reserved** opens **Remove direct public network**: the address is kept as a Reserved IP for later reuse, and the VM switches to its NAT VPC interface for outbound internet. Direct inbound traffic to the address stops, so add a NAT port-forwarding rule for services that must stay reachable.
* **Attach IP** / **Attach or Move IP** — attach one of your same-location Reserved IPs, or move one from another VM. A Reserved IP can be attached to one VM at a time.
* **Detach IP** — public traffic to that address stops; the address stays in **Reserved IPs**.
* **Repair network** — shown only for an older VM that has no active network interface. Click it to repair the VM's provider network, then attach a Reserved IP.

When you delete a VM, the delete dialog also offers to keep its public IP as a Reserved IP — see [Power actions](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/power-actions#delete).

### VPC Networks

Lists the VPC interfaces attached to the VM, with each interface's private IP, subnet, and VPC ID:

* **Attach VPC** — connect the VM to a VPC and subnet in the same site. In the panel, pick the **VPC** and **Subnet**, choose **Private IP assignment** (**Automatic**, or **Specific address** for an unused host address in the subnet), check **Traffic routing**, then click **Attach VPC**. If the VM has no network yet, the VPC becomes its primary network. If it already has one, the new VPC carries private traffic only — except a NAT VPC, where you can choose **Use VPC for internet** (the VPC becomes the default route; the current public IP stays until you remove it under **IPv4 & Reserved IP**) or **Private traffic only**.
* **Detach VPC** — remove a VPC interface. A VM must always keep at least one network interface, so the primary interface can't be detached until another route is in place. The guest may need network configuration after the change.

## Connecting to private VMs

**Private + NAT** and **Private only** VMs can't accept direct connections from the internet. **Overview → Connection Details** shows the private SSH or RDP command to use from inside the VPC — for example through a VPN, a bastion host, or another VM in the VPC. NAT VMs can also use a NAT port-forward rule for inbound access.

## DNS

Use any DNS provider to point a domain at your VM:

1. Add an `A` record for the VM's public IP.
2. Add a `CNAME` for `www` if needed.

A [Reserved IP](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management/reserved-ips) keeps the address stable if you later replace the VM.

## Bandwidth and overage

Each plan includes a monthly outbound bandwidth allowance (for example **2 TB** on `std.1.c2.m8`). The Monitoring tab's **Network Traffic** chart shows current inbound and outbound throughput and your monthly outbound usage.

* Inbound traffic is unmetered.
* Outbound usage above the included allowance is billed per GB; see your plan summary for the rate.

## Load balancing

To put a load balancer in front of multiple VMs, use [Load Balancer](/docs/network-security/load-balancer):

* Create the load balancer in the same region as your VMs.
* Attach the VMs as backends and configure a health check.
* Optionally terminate TLS at the load balancer.

## Troubleshooting

**VM has no public IP after deploy**
**Private + NAT** and **Private only** VMs don't get a public IP — this is expected. For **Public IP** VMs, refresh the list; the column updates after provisioning completes. If it stays blank for more than a few minutes, check [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs) for a failed create.

**Can't SSH but the VM is Running**

* Check that the VM's firewall group allows port 22 from your address.
* Confirm you're using the username and host from **Overview → Connection Details**.
* If the key is wrong or lost, add another saved key, or reset the password and enable password login, on **Settings → Access**. Browser console access isn't available in the portal yet.

**Deploy says a Reserved IP is required**
You chose **Public IP** with a **private** VPC. Create a Reserved IP in the same location, or pick a public VPC or **No VPC**.

**Bandwidth chart looks flat or empty**
The chart smooths over its time range. Switch to **30m** for short-window detail.

## Related pages

* [Create a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/create-a-vm)
* [VPC](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management)
* [Reserved IPs](/docs/network-security/vpc-ip-management/reserved-ips)
* [Firewalls](/docs/network-security/firewalls)
* [Load Balancer](/docs/network-security/load-balancer)

title: Attach volumes

# Attach volumes

> Add Block Storage volumes to a Cloud VM and mount them inside the guest.

Attach a [Block Storage](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage) volume to a Cloud VM when you need persistent storage that survives plan changes and VM deletion (deleting a VM detaches its data volumes automatically and keeps them). Volumes attach as additional disks (`vdb`, `vdc`, …) alongside the root disk (`vda`).

## When to use a separate volume

* Your data should outlive the VM (databases, file servers, user uploads).
* You want to grow capacity independently of CPU and RAM.
* You need to move data between VMs (detach from one, attach to another).
* You want snapshot scope flexibility — capture data volumes selectively ([Selective volumes capture mode](/docs/tools/snapshots/create-a-snapshot)).

For ephemeral data that lives and dies with the VM, the included root disk on each [instance type](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/instance-types) is fine.

## Attach a volume

### 1. Create the volume

If you don't already have one, create a volume in the **same region** as the VM. See [Create a volume](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage/create-a-volume).

### 2. Attach from Block Storage

Volumes are attached from the **Block Storage** page — the VM detail page doesn't have a volumes section. Open **Block Storage**, click the volume, then click **Attach to Server** and pick the VM. See [Attach and detach a volume](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage/attach-and-detach-a-volume) for the full steps.

### 3. Wait for the attachment to complete

When the attachment finishes, the volume shows the VM as attached in **Block Storage**, and it appears as a new block device inside the guest. The operation is also recorded in [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs).

## Mount the volume inside the guest (Linux)

Use the commands on the volume's **Mount Instructions** tab in **Block Storage**, or follow these standard steps the first time you attach a fresh volume.

```bash
# 1. Confirm the new device
lsblk

# 2. (First time only) Create a filesystem
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vdb

# 3. Create a mount point
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/volume_<id>

# 4. Mount it
sudo mount /dev/vdb /mnt/volume_<id>

# 5. Persist across reboots — use UUID for stability
echo "UUID=$(blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/vdb) /mnt/volume_<id> ext4 defaults 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
```

> **Warning**
>
> **Use UUID-based fstab entries.** Device names like `/dev/vdb` can change after detach/reattach or restore. Mounting by UUID keeps the path stable.

After a restore, the recovery point's **Details** view (on the VM's **Snapshots** or **Backups** tab) shows **Mount Instructions** for each restored data volume. A restored volume already has a filesystem — mount it, don't format it.

## Mount the volume inside the guest (Windows)

1. Open **Disk Management**.
2. Bring the new disk **Online** and **Initialize** it (GPT for >2 TB).
3. Right-click the unallocated space → **New Simple Volume** and follow the wizard.
4. Assign a drive letter and format as NTFS.

## Detach a volume

1. Unmount inside the guest first (`sudo umount /mnt/volume_<id>`) to avoid filesystem corruption.
2. On the volume's **Block Storage** page, click **Detach**.
3. Wait for the volume to show as detached in **Block Storage**.

A detached volume keeps its data and can be reattached to any VM in the same region.

## Volumes and snapshots

When you take a snapshot, you choose the **Capture Mode**:

| Mode                     | What's captured                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Root volume only**     | Just the boot disk. Attached data volumes are skipped.            |
| **All attached volumes** | Root disk plus every attached data volume.                        |
| **Selective volumes**    | Root is always included; pick which attached data volumes to add. |

After restore, captured data volumes are auto-attached to the target VM. Mount instructions are surfaced in the snapshot detail view. See [Create a snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/create-a-snapshot).

## Troubleshooting

**`lsblk` doesn't show the new device**
Wait 10–20 seconds after the attachment completes, then rerun. If it still doesn't appear, reboot the VM.

**`mount` fails with "wrong fs type"**
The volume isn't formatted yet. Run `sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vdX` on the **first** attach only.

**Volume is read-only after restore**
The platform restores the volume but doesn't mount it inside the guest. Use the **Mount Instructions** in the recovery point's **Details** view for that volume.

## Related pages

* [Block Storage overview](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage)
* [Create a volume](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage/create-a-volume)
* [Attach and detach a volume](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage/attach-and-detach-a-volume)
* [Create a snapshot](/docs/tools/snapshots/create-a-snapshot)

# Monitoring

> Track CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics for your Cloud VM, and find its recent operations in Activity logs.

The **Monitoring** tab on the server detail page shows live metrics for the VM. Use it to spot saturation, validate resize impact, and see the load of backup or snapshot windows.

## Open monitoring

1. Go to **Cloud VMs** in the IBEE Solutions portal.
2. Click your VM to open the detail page.
3. Open the **Monitoring** tab.

The header shows when metrics were last updated and the sample interval (typically **1-minute intervals**). Use the time range buttons to switch between **30m**, **1h**, **6h**, **24h**, and **7d**. Click **Refresh** to force an immediate sample.

## Compute metrics

| Metric                 | Source                             | What it shows                                                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **CPU Utilization**    | Host-side libvirt                  | VM CPU % across all allocated vCPUs. Spikes above the plan's vCPU count indicate steal pressure.   |
| **Memory Utilization** | Host-side libvirt (when available) | Memory used vs. allocated, in MB. Falls back to balloon stats when the guest agent is unavailable. |

A current value and last sample timestamp are shown above each chart.

## Storage and disk metrics

| Metric                  | Source                 | What it shows                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Storage Utilization** | QEMU guest agent       | Guest filesystem usage as a percentage and absolute used/total. Requires the guest agent to be installed. |
| **Disk Throughput**     | libvirt block counters | Read and write throughput (B/s, KB/s, MB/s).                                                              |
| **Disk IOPS**           | libvirt block counters | Read and write operations per second.                                                                     |

If **Storage Utilization** is missing, install or start `qemu-guest-agent` inside the VM:

```bash
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-guest-agent
sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
```

Throughput and IOPS metrics work without the guest agent.

## Network metrics

The **Network Traffic** chart plots **inbound** and **outbound** traffic per second, with the current rates and your **Monthly outbound** usage shown above it. Use it together with the bandwidth allowance for your plan ([Instance types](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/instance-types)) to estimate monthly egress.

## Recent activity

The Monitoring tab shows metrics only. To see what was done to a VM — create, power actions, volume changes, snapshots, restores — and whether each operation succeeded, open **Activity Logs** under **Organization** in the portal sidebar. See [Activity logs](/docs/platform-fundamentals/activity-logs).

## Use the API

The same metrics are in the public API (GPU VMs use the same paths under `/compute/gpu-vms/{vm_id}`):

* `GET /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/metrics` — current values.
* `GET /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/metrics/timeseries` — time series for a range.
* `GET /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/metrics/bandwidth` — monthly bandwidth.
* `GET /compute/cloud-vms/{vm_id}/events` — the VM's recent events (API only).

## Tips

* Investigate **CPU sustained above 80%** before resizing — many workloads are I/O- or memory-bound.
* A flat **Memory Utilization** line near 100% with low free RAM is a strong signal to upsize.
* If **Disk Throughput** plateaus while CPU has headroom, you may be hitting the disk's IOPS ceiling — consider attaching faster [Block Storage](/docs/infrastructure/block-storage).
* Use the **24h** range to see backup or snapshot windows; expect a small CPU and disk bump during those windows.

## Related pages

* [Instance types](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/instance-types)
* [Resize a VM](/docs/infrastructure/cloud-vms/resize-a-vm)
* [Backups](/docs/tools/backups)
* [Snapshots](/docs/tools/snapshots)

# Object Storage

> IBEE Object Storage is a scalable, S3-compatible storage service for files, media, backups, and application assets. Works with any S3-compatible SDK or tool.

IBEE Object Storage is a scalable object storage service with an S3-compatible API. Use it to store files, media, backups, and application assets — accessible from any S3-compatible SDK, CLI tool, or client.

## Use cases

* **Static website hosting** — serve HTML, CSS, and assets directly from a bucket
* **Media and asset storage** — store images, videos, and documents for your applications
* **Application data and backups** — store database dumps, snapshots, and application exports
* **Log archiving** — collect and retain logs at scale
* **CDN origin storage** — use a bucket as the origin for CDN-delivered content

## Capabilities

| Feature             | Description                                                                                                   |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| S3-compatible API   | Works with AWS SDKs, s3cmd, rclone, and other S3-compatible clients                                           |
| S3 credentials      | Access Key ID + Secret Access Key per workspace, created under **Organization → API Tokens → S3 Credentials** |
| Public Access URL   | Serve a bucket publicly without an SDK                                                                        |
| Custom Domains      | Front a public bucket with your own hostname                                                                  |
| CORS                | Cross-origin browser access rules per bucket                                                                  |
| Lifecycle Policies  | Automate object expiry                                                                                        |
| Versioning          | Keep previous object versions (turned on with Object Lock at bucket creation)                                 |
| Object Lock         | Make objects immutable for compliance (set at bucket creation), plus per-object retention and legal hold      |
| Event Notifications | Webhook when objects are uploaded                                                                             |

## Available regions

| Region code | Location               | Status                                            |
| ----------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| VGA         | Amaravati, India       | Available                                         |
| HYD         | Hyderabad, India       | Pre-order — [contact sales](mailto:sales@ibee.ai) |
| IAD         | Ashburn, United States | Pre-order — [contact sales](mailto:sales@ibee.ai) |

## Where to start

#### [Core Concepts](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/core-concepts)

Buckets, objects, regions, endpoints — the building blocks.

#### [Upload Your First Object](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/upload-your-first-object)

Create your first bucket, generate API credentials, and upload an object.

#### [Buckets](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/buckets)

Containers for objects — settings, policies, lifecycle, CORS, custom domains.

#### [Objects](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/objects)

Upload, download, lock, and presign objects.

#### [Mount a Bucket as a Filesystem](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/mount-a-bucket-as-a-filesystem)

Access a bucket like a local directory with `s3fs` or `rclone`.

#### [Metrics](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/metrics)

Track usage, objects, and bandwidth — organization-wide and per bucket.

* [Static Site Hosting](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/static-site-hosting)
* [CDN integration](/docs/infrastructure/object-storage/cdn-integration)

description: Core building blocks of IBEE Object Storage — buckets, objects, regions, endpoints, and access.
